summary: Describes a formal process for defining and standardizing new service types and their attributes for use with the service: URL scheme in the Service Location Protocol.

plainLanguage.summary: This document defines the service: URL, a way to write the address of a network service, and a template format for describing new kinds of service. A template lists the attributes a service of that kind carries, so a program can pick the service that suits it and read the attributes correctly.

subtitle: A formal template format for describing new service types and their attributes in service: URLs.

tldr.problem: The Service Location Protocol lets a client find services by type, but clients need to know which of several services of the same type to pick, and that knowledge needs a shared, formal definition.
tldr.mechanism: The document defines the service: URL scheme and a template format, written in ABNF, that describes a service type, its URL syntax and its attributes with types, flags, defaults and allowed values.
tldr.outcome: New service types can be standardized through a defined process, with IANA holding a registry of templates and every version archived, so that tools can parse registrations and applications can translate attribute strings.

today: RFC 2609 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 2165, and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes it. The service: URL scheme and the template format it defines are the ones used with the Service Location Protocol version 2 in RFC 2608.

sections.title: What the Document Adds
sections.content:
The document describes a URL scheme, called service: URL, which defines network access information for network services using a formal notation. It also describes how to define a set of attributes to associate with a service: URL. These attributes let end users and programs select between network services of the same type that have different capabilities. The attributes are defined in a template document that is readable by people and by machines.

A client uses attributes to select a particular service. Service selection happens by obtaining the service: URL that offers the right configuration for the client. Service type templates define the syntax of service: URLs for a particular service type, as well as the attributes that accompany a service: URL in a service registration.

Templates serve four distinct purposes. For standardization, the template is reviewed before it is standardized, and once it is, all versions of it are archived by IANA. For service registration, servers making use of the Service Location Protocol register themselves and their attributes, using the templates to generate the registrations; in registering, the service must use the specified values for its attributes. For client presentation, client applications may display service information, and the template provides type information and explanatory text that may help in producing user interfaces. For internationalization, entities with access to the template for a given service type in two different languages may translate between the two languages, though a service may register itself in more than one language using templates, and it has been configured by an operator who registered service attributes in a single language.

The Service Location Protocol version 2 allows service: URLs to be registered and discovered, though they may also be used in other contexts. Client applications discover service registrations by issuing queries for services of a particular type, specifying the attributes of the service: URLs to return. Clients retrieve the attributes of a particular service by supplying its service: URL, and attributes for all registrations of a particular type can also be retrieved. Services may register themselves, or registrations may be made on their behalf, and these registrations contain a service: URL, possibly attributes, and possibly digital signatures.
sections.plainLanguage: When several servers offer the same kind of service, a program needs a way to say which one it wants. This document gives that way: a template that lists the attributes a service of that kind carries, and a URL form that points at the service.

sections.title: The service: URL Syntax
sections.content:
The syntax of a service: URL MUST conform to an absolute URI. It differs enough from a generic URI that it is best to be treated as an opaque URI unless a specific parser for it is available. All service: URLs have the same syntax up to the url-part, and the syntax for the rest depends on the service type that follows the service scheme. All service: URLs have a service access point portion, indicating the address of the service to access, and the syntax for that field depends on the service type definition.

The ABNF for a service: URL is:

service: URL    =   "service:" service-type ":" sap
service-type    =   abstract-type ":" url-scheme / concrete-type
abstract-type   =   type-name [ "." naming-auth ]
concrete-type   =   protocol [ "." naming-auth ]
type-name       =   resname
naming-auth     =   resname
url-scheme      =   resname
resname         =   ALPHA [ 1*(ALPHA / DIGIT / "+" / "-") ]
sap             =   site [url-part]
site            =   ipsite / atsite / ipxsite
ipsite          =   "//" [ [ user "@" ] hostport ]
hostport        =   host [ ":" port ]
host            =   hostname / hostnumber
hostname        =   *( domainlabel "." ) toplabel
hostnumber      =   ipv4-number
ipv4-number     =   1*3DIGIT 3("." 1*3DIGIT)
port            =   1*DIGIT
url-part        =   [ url-path ] [ attr-list ]
url-path        =   1 * ( "/" *xchar )
attr-list       =   1 * ( ";" attr-asgn )
attr-asgn       =   attr-id / attr-id "=" attr-value

Although both upper case and lower case characters are recognized in the service-type field for convenience, the name is case-folded into lower case, so service types are not distinguished on the basis of case and "http" and "HTTP" designate the same service type.

Besides the AppleTalk grammar, some characters must be escaped before use, and to escape any character the two digits indicating its ASCII value are preceded by a percent sign.
sections.plainLanguage: The URL starts with the word service, then the kind of service, then the address to reach it. The address can be a host name, an IP address, or an IPX or AppleTalk address, and a port number may follow.

sections.title: Attributes and Where They Live
sections.content:
The service scheme-specific information following the service: URL scheme identifier provides the information necessary to access the service. The form of a service: URL is service: URL = "service:" service-type ":" site url-path, where the site refers to an ipsite, ipxsite or atsite depending on whether the URL locates an IP, IPX or AppleTalk service access point.

The ipsite field is typically either a domain name or an IP network protocol address for the service, and possibly a port number. Use of DNS hostnames is preferred for ease of renumbering. The site field can be null if other information in the service URL or service attributes is sufficient to use the service. The sap field allows more information to be provided, by way of the url-path and the attribute list, that can uniquely locate the service or resource if the site is not sufficient for that purpose.

An attribute list field appears at the end of the url-part field, but is never required to exist in any service location registration. It is composed of a list of semicolon-separated attribute assignments of the form attr-id "=" attr-value, or for keyword attributes just attr-id. Attributes are part of a service: URL when the attributes are required to access a particular service. For instance, an ACAP service might require that the client authenticate with it through Kerberos, and including an attribute in the service registration lets the ACAP client use the correct SASL authentication mechanism. The example given is service:acap://some.where.net;authentication=KERBEROSV4.

Attributes associated with a service: URL are not typically included in the service: URL itself. They are stored and retrieved using other mechanisms: the service: URL is uniquely identified with a particular service agent or resource and is used when registering or requesting the attribute information.
sections.plainLanguage: Some attributes have to live inside the URL because a client cannot use the service without them, such as how to authenticate. Most attributes are kept elsewhere and looked up using the URL, which is why a registration can carry more information than the URL shows.

sections.title: Abstract and Concrete Service Types
sections.content:
An abstract service type is a service type that can be implemented by a variety of different service agents. To register a service: URL for an abstract service type, the abstract-type grammar rule is used, which produces a URL that includes enough information to use the service, namely the protocol, address and path information. Unlike a concrete service: URL, however, the service type is not enough to determine the service access; rather, an abstract service type denotes a class of service types.

Concrete service templates inherit all attributes defined in the abstract service template from which the concrete template was derived. An attribute defined in the abstract service template MUST not be defined in the concrete service template as well, which simplifies the interpretation of templates. For example, if an abstract service template for the service type 'Abstract' defines an attribute FOO, all concrete service templates derived from it, such as 'Abstract:Concrete', implicitly include the definition of attribute FOO, and the derived template MUST NOT redefine FOO.

Some services make use of several protocols that are in common use and are distinct services in their own right, and in these cases an abstract service type is appropriate. What is essential is that all the required information for the service is clearly defined. The document's example is a network service for dynamically loading device drivers, where the client needs the protocol used to load the driver code, a pathname identifying where the code is located, and the name of the driver. Rather than forming the first two items into a URL and embedding that in a service: URL, an abstract service type SHOULD be used: the service type is not "ftp" but "device-drivers", and the URL becomes service:device-drivers:ftp://x3.bean.org/drivers/diskdrivers.drv;driver=scsi;platform=sys3.2-rs3000. Other URLs for the same service using other protocols are also supported, such as the same URL with tftp or http instead of ftp. Using SLP, a search for the service type "device-drivers" may return all three URLs, and the client selects the most appropriate access protocol for the desired resource.

The fundamental requirement is that the abstract service type MUST be well specified, so that program code or human users have enough information to access the service. In every case, a well-specified abstract type includes either an access protocol and a network address where the service is available, or an embedded URL for a standardized URL scheme that describes how to access the service.
sections.plainLanguage: Some jobs can be done over more than one protocol. The document lets you name the job itself, such as device-drivers, and put the protocol inside the URL. A search for the job then returns every copy, and the client picks the protocol it wants.

sections.title: Defining an Attribute
sections.content:
An attribute definition precisely specifies the attribute's type, other restrictions on it such as whether it is multi-valued or optional, some text readable by people describing the attribute, and lists of default and allowed values. The only required information is the attribute's type; the rest are optional.

An attribute definition has five components in order of appearance: an attribute identifier that acts as the name of the attribute; attribute descriptors, which are the type and flags; an optional list of values assigned to the attribute by default; an optional block of text readable by people giving a short, informative description of the attribute; and an optional list of allowed values restricting the value or values the attribute can take on. The definition begins with the identifier and ends with a single empty line.

Attributes can have one of five types. String, signed integer and boolean have the standard programming language or database semantics. Integers are restricted to signed values that can be represented in 32 bits. The character set used to represent strings is not specified when the template is defined, but is determined by the service registration. Booleans have the standard syntax. Opaque values are byte-escaped values that can represent any other kind of data. Keyword attributes have no characteristics other than their existence, and possibly the descriptive text in their definition. Keyword attribute definitions MUST have no flag information after the type definition, nor any default or allowed values list. Boolean attributes are single value only; multi-valued boolean attributes are not allowed.

Flags determine other characteristics of an attribute. With the exception of keyword attributes, which may not have any flags, flags follow the attribute type on the same line as the identifier, are separated from each other by whitespace, and may appear in any order. The flag o or O indicates that the attribute is optional; without it, the attribute is required in every service registration. The flag m or M indicates that the attribute can take on multiple values, in which case every value has the same type as the type given in the definition; boolean attributes must not include this flag. The flag l or L indicates that the attribute is literal, that is, not meant to be translated into other languages, and an attribute with this flag is not considered readable by people. The flag x or X indicates that clients SHOULD include the attribute in requests for services, because neglecting it will not sufficiently differentiate the service.

The values for multi-valued attributes are an unordered set. Deletions of individual values from a multi-valued attribute are not supported, and deleting the attribute causes the entire set of values to be removed.
sections.plainLanguage: Each attribute has a name, a type such as string, integer, boolean or opaque, and up to four flags. The flags say whether the attribute is optional, whether it may hold several values, whether its text should be left untranslated, and whether a client should ask for it when searching.

sections.title: Languages and Translation
sections.content:
The service: URL must be encoded using the general URI rules, and the character set encoding is limited to specific ranges within the US-ASCII character set. The template itself is encoded in UTF-8 characters.

The language used in attribute strings should be identified by supplying a Language Tag in the service template submission. A program can translate a service registration from one language to another provided it has both the template of the language for the registration and the template of the desired target language. All standardized attributes are in the same order in both templates, and all non-arbitrary strings, including the descriptive help text, is directly translatable.

Non-literal attribute definitions, attribute identifiers, attribute type names, attribute flags and the boolean constants "true" and "false" are never translated. Translation of attribute identifiers is prohibited, because as with domain names they can potentially be part of a service: URL and therefore their character set is restricted, and as with variable identifiers in programming languages they could become embedded into program code. All strings used in attribute values are assumed translatable unless explicitly defined as being literal, so that best effort translation does not modify strings meant to be interpreted by a program rather than a person.

There are two ways to go about translation: standardization and best effort. When the service type is standardized, more than one document can be submitted for review. One service type description is approved as a master, so that when a service type template is updated in one language, all the translations, at least eventually, reflect the same semantics. If no document exists describing the standard translation of the service type, a best effort translation for strings should be done.
sections.plainLanguage: Attribute text can be written in more than one language. The names of attributes and the flags stay the same in every language, because programs use them, while the descriptive text is translated.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
Service type templates provide information that is used to interpret information obtained by the Service Location Protocol. If these templates are modified, or false templates are distributed, services may not correctly register themselves, or clients might not be able to interpret service information.

The service: URLs themselves specify the service access point and protocol for a particular service type. These URLs could be distributed and indicate the location of a service other than the one normally wanted. The Service Location Protocol distributes service: URLs and has an authentication mechanism that allows the URLs of registered services to be signed and for the signatures to be verified by clients.

Each service template will include a security considerations section describing security issues with using the service scheme for the specific service type.
sections.plainLanguage: A template is what tells a program how to read a service's information, so a wrong or altered template makes clients misread what they are told. Signed registrations are the defence the document points to.

data.title: ABNF for a service: URL
data.code:
service: URL    =   "service:" service-type ":" sap
service-type    =   abstract-type ":" url-scheme / concrete-type
sap             =   site [url-part]
site            =   ipsite / atsite / ipxsite
ipsite          =   "//" [ [ user "@" ] hostport ]
hostport        =   host [ ":" port ]
url-part        =   [ url-path ] [ attr-list ]
attr-list       =   1 * ( ";" attr-asgn )
attr-asgn       =   attr-id / attr-id "=" attr-value

No; the protocol sits inside the URL instead.
Defined in the abstract template and inherited by every concrete template derived from it.

items.label: String type
items.desc: Standard programming language or database semantics. The character set is set by the registration, not the template.

items.label: Integer type
items.desc: Signed values that can be represented in 32 bits.

items.label: Boolean type
items.desc: Standard syntax. Single value only; multi-valued booleans are not allowed.

items.label: Opaque type
items.desc: Byte-escaped values that can represent any other kind of data.

items.label: Keyword type
items.desc: No characteristics other than existence. No flags, no default or allowed values list.

items.label: Optional flag
items.desc: The attribute is optional. Without it the attribute is required in every registration.

items.label: Multi-valued flag
items.desc: The attribute can take on multiple values, all of the same type.

items.label: Literal flag
items.desc: The attribute is not meant to be translated into other languages.

items.label: Required in queries flag
items.desc: Clients SHOULD include the attribute in requests for services.

viz.caption: THE FOUR PURPOSES OF A TEMPLATE

items.title: Standardization
items.text: The template is reviewed before it is standardized, and all versions are archived by IANA.

items.title: Service registration
items.text: Servers use the templates to generate their registrations, using the specified values for their attributes.

items.title: Client presentation
items.text: Applications display service information using the type information and explanatory text the template provides.

items.title: Internationalization
items.text: Entities with the template in two languages may translate between them.
